title: Kanishka's Sword on the Silk Road

title_i18n.en: Kanishka's Sword on the Silk Road

subtitle: When the Kushan Banner Met the Ancient Roads of the World
era: Reign of Kanishka I, c. 127-150 CE by Falk's dating
region: Purushapura, Mathura, Kashmir, the Tarim Basin and the Gangetic plain
moral: Power is widest when it protects the roads it conquers.

sources.citation: Rabatak inscription, Cribb and Sims-Williams, JONS 160 (1995/96); revised by Sims-Williams (2008)
sources.note: Primary Bactrian evidence for Kanishka's genealogy and claimed eastern cities.

sources.citation: Hou Hanshu chapters 47 and 88, trans. John Hill (2009)
sources.note: Chinese record of Kushan-Han conflict and Central Asian context.

sources.citation: Harry Falk, The Yuga of Sphujiddhvaja and the Era of the Kushans, Silk Road Art and Archaeology 7 (2001)
sources.note: Influential argument for 127 CE as Year 1 of the Kanishka era.

dialogue.text: In the age of Kanishka I, c. 127–150 CE, a Kushan king of kings bent the Silk Road around his throne at Purushapura.
From Sindh and the Indus, across Kashmir to the Tarim Basin and down toward Saketa and Pataliputra, old roads carried silk, ideas and the ambitions of empires.
Around 127 CE, as Harry Falk’s dating now suggests, Kanishka made Purushapura his chief seat and fashioned himself not a border chief, but a king over the great routes.

panels.shot: medium close-up on coin in hand

dialogue.text: On his coins, separated from later Kanishkas by numismatic study, he stands clad in Kushan dress, sword at his side, styling himself in Bactrian as king of kings.
In Bactrian words at Rabatak, he named his forefathers and claimed rule from the lands of Sindh eastward to Saketa, Kausambi, Pataliputra and Sri-Champa.
The Rabatak inscription, lost for centuries and only revealed in 1993, transformed our sense of his reach, showing eastern cities under his authority or submission.

panels.shot: sweeping wide of army and caravan

dialogue.text: His sword opened space for traders and pilgrims. Armies marched not only to seize land, but to steady the roads on which wealth and reputation flowed.
To hold the high routes toward the Tarim Basin meant braving mountain passes where one misstep could end a caravan, yet where control meant a share in distant markets.
Chinese chronicles, in the Hou Hanshu, speak of Kushan power pressing toward the Tarim corridors, where Han interests already strained against local kings and steppe rivals.

panels.shot: dramatic wide of opposing hosts at distance

dialogue.text: Across these high paths, Kushan and Han claims met. Chinese court records remember conflict, though the precise battles live only in their telling, not in Kushan words.

panels.shot: close-up profile as he looks toward mountains

dialogue.text: If I hold the road, I hold the world between oceans.
When power steadied such roads, markets thickened. Coins with his name passed from the Indus to oasis towns, turning conquest into daily exchange.
Along these routes, gods travelled too. Under his rule, Iranian, Indian and foreign cults found room, and stories crossed mountains with traders and teachers.
Rabatak’s carved lines list Saketa, Kausambi, Pataliputra and Sri-Champa among his eastern domains, though how he gained their obedience remains hidden from us.

panels.shot: wide shot of Ganga plain city from afar

dialogue.text: We can say his authority reached these old centres, but not that he destroyed them. The stone bears his claim, not the smoke of Pataliputra’s fall.
The surest trace of his reach lies in metal. Coins marked his authority more gently than spears, binding distant buyers and sellers to a king they would never see.

panels.shot: melancholic wide, king overlooking caravan at dusk

dialogue.text: In time, campaigns end, borders shift and names fade, yet the roads endure. A ruler’s harsh edge can widen into a shield for those who walk them.

panels.shot: extreme close-up on weathered stone inscription

dialogue.text: Today, we read Rabatak’s lines and the Hou Hanshu’s records and see Kanishka’s age as one where a Kushan sword and a network of roads shaped the meeting of India and the wider world.
